<h2>What is an algorithm, and what does a computer do with it?</h2>
<p>
  Every time you follow a recipe, give someone directions to your house, or work through long division, you are running an algorithm. You start with an input, you follow a fixed sequence of steps, and you end up with a result. Computer science takes that same everyday idea and asks a tighter question: what is the precise, unambiguous list of steps that solves this problem, and how do we hand those steps to a machine that has zero common sense?
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Definition</h4>
  <p>An <strong>algorithm</strong> is a step-by-step process for completing a task or solving a problem. Algorithms can be represented in written language, in diagrams (like flowcharts), or in a programming language. <strong>Sequencing</strong> is the part of an algorithm that defines the order in which steps are performed, one step at a time.</p>
</div>

<p>
  AP CSA is, at its core, a course about writing algorithms in Java. Before any code is involved, though, the algorithm has to exist as a clear, ordered plan. The CED is explicit about this: students should be able to <em>represent patterns and algorithms found in everyday life</em>, not just type Java. The reason is practical. Programmers who can’t describe their plan in plain English usually can’t describe it in Java either. They end up debugging a mental model that was never coherent to begin with.
</p>

<h3>Sequencing: one step at a time, in a specific order</h3>
<p>
  Sequencing sounds obvious until you try to break it. Consider making a peanut butter sandwich. “Spread the peanut butter, take out the bread, open the jar” lists all the right ingredients but produces a mess. The same is true in code. <code>System.out.println(name); String name = "Tanner";</code> uses the right pieces but compiles only if reordered. Computers execute statements <strong>one at a time, in the order written</strong>, with no ability to look ahead or guess what you meant.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Example</h4>
  <p>Algorithm for “log in to a website”: (1) open the login page, (2) type the username, (3) type the password, (4) click submit, (5) wait for the server response, (6) display the home page <em>only if</em> the response was successful. Swap steps 3 and 4 and the password is never entered. Swap steps 4 and 5 and the user clicks submit before there’s anything to submit. The steps haven’t changed; only the sequence has, and the sequence is what makes it work.</p>
</div>

<h3>From algorithm to running program: writing, compiling, executing</h3>
<p>
  Once you have an algorithm, you write it in a programming language. Java code can be written in any text editor, but most programmers use an <strong>integrated development environment (IDE)</strong>, a single application that lets you write the code, compile it, and run it without leaving the window. Common AP CSA classroom IDEs include IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, BlueJ, and Replit. The CED treats the choice of IDE as classroom-dependent and not tested directly, what <em>is</em> tested is what the IDE does for you.
</p>
<p>
  The key step is <strong>compilation</strong>. A <strong>compiler</strong> is a program that translates your Java source code into a form the machine can run, and along the way it checks the code for certain kinds of errors. If the compiler finds an error, your program does not run at all. You must fix the error first. This is one of the most important ideas in this lesson: <em>the compiler is a gatekeeper for one class of mistakes, but it is blind to others</em>.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout warning">
  <h4>Common misconception</h4>
  <p>“If my code compiles, it works.” This is wrong, and the AP exam tests it directly. The compiler only catches errors related to the rules of the Java language (missing semicolons, undeclared variables, type mismatches). A program can compile cleanly, run end-to-end, and still produce the wrong answer because the <em>logic</em>, the algorithm you wrote, is flawed. Successful compilation means “Java accepts this as valid Java,” not “this solves your problem.”</p>
</div>

<h3>The four error types you must distinguish</h3>
<p>
  The CED is unusually specific here. Topic 1.1.C names four error categories, and the AP exam tests whether you can place a given mistake into the right bucket. The distinctions matter because they tell you <em>when</em> an error will surface: at compile time, at run time, or only when you happen to test with the right input.
</p>
<ul>
  <li>A <strong>syntax error</strong> is a violation of the rules of the Java language. Missing semicolon, misspelled keyword, unclosed brace. The compiler catches every syntax error. Your program does not run.</li>
  <li>A <strong>logic error</strong> is a mistake in the algorithm itself. The code compiles and runs but produces wrong output. You only catch logic errors by testing with specific inputs and comparing actual output to expected output.</li>
  <li>A <strong>run-time error</strong> is a problem that occurs <em>during execution</em>. The compiler accepted the code, but something goes wrong while the program is running, usually causing it to terminate abnormally.</li>
  <li>An <strong>exception</strong> is a specific type of run-time error: an unexpected condition that the compiler couldn’t predict, which interrupts the normal flow of execution. <code>ArithmeticException</code> from dividing by zero and <code>NullPointerException</code> from calling a method on <code>null</code> are the two you’ll see most often in Unit 1.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout key-insight">
  <h4>Key insight</h4>
  <p>The compiler catches <em>syntax</em> errors only. Logic, run-time, and exception errors all slip past the compiler. They require running the program (and often testing with specific inputs) to surface. This is why writing test cases is part of programming, not an optional extra.</p>
</div>

<h3>Key vocabulary</h3>
<table class="apcsa-vocab">
  <thead>
    <tr>
<th style="width: 28% !important;">Term</th>
<th>Definition</th>
</tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Algorithm</strong></td>
<td>A step-by-step process for completing a task or solving a problem, representable in written language, diagrams, or code.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Sequencing</strong></td>
<td>The order in which steps in a process are completed; steps run one at a time.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>IDE</strong></td>
<td>Integrated Development Environment, an application that bundles tools to write, compile, and run code in one place.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Compiler</strong></td>
<td>A program that translates source code into a runnable form and checks for certain language-rule errors before the program runs.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Syntax error</strong></td>
<td>A mistake that violates the rules of the programming language; detected by the compiler. The program does not run.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Logic error</strong></td>
<td>A mistake in the algorithm that causes incorrect or unexpected behavior; detected only by testing with specific inputs.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Run-time error</strong></td>
<td>A mistake that occurs during program execution, typically causing the program to terminate abnormally.</td>
</tr>
    <tr>
<td><strong>Exception</strong></td>
<td>A type of run-time error caused by an unexpected condition the compiler did not detect; interrupts the normal flow of execution.</td>
</tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

    id: 'p1',

    prompt: 'This should print <code>Hello, AP CSA</code> but will not compile. Fix it so it runs.',

}`,
    expected: `Hello, AP CSA`,
    hint: 'Every Java statement ends with the same punctuation mark. Read the print line all the way to the end.'
  },
  {
    id: 'p2',
    title: 'Problem 2 of 3 — fix the bug',
    prompt: 'A program runs steps in order. This should print <code>First</code> then <code>Second</code>, but the lines come out reversed. Fix the order.',
    starter: `public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        System.out.println("Second");
        System.out.println("First");
    }
}`,
    expected: `First
Second`,
    hint: 'Statements run top to bottom, in the order you write them. Which line does the expected output show first?'
  },
  {
    id: 'p3',
    title: 'Problem 3 of 3 — write from spec',
    prompt: 'Write code that prints exactly two lines: <code>Algorithm</code> on the first line and <code>Program</code> on the second.',
    starter: `public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        // print Algorithm, then Program, each on its own line

    }
}`,
    expected: `Algorithm
Program`,
    hint: 'Each print-line statement puts its output on its own line. How many lines does the expected output have, and so how many statements do you need?'
  }
];

  var editors = {};

  function normalize(s) {
    if (!s) {
      return '';
    }
    return s.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n').split('\n').map(function(line){
      return line.replace(/\s+$/, '');
    }).join('\n').replace(/\n+$/, '');
  }

  function el(tag, cls, html) {
    var node = document.createElement(tag);
    if (cls) {
      node.className = cls;
    }
    if (html !== undefined) {
      node.innerHTML = html;
    }
    return node;
  }

  function buildProblem(p, idx) {
    var card = el('div', 'csa-ce-problem');
    card.appendChild(el('div', 'csa-ce-num', p.title));
    card.appendChild(el('div', 'csa-ce-prompt', p.prompt));

    var edWrap = el('div', 'csa-ce-editor');
    var ta = document.createElement('textarea');

    var cm = CodeMirror.fromTextArea(ta, {

    });
    editors[p.id] = cm;
    setTimeout(function(){ cm.refresh(); }, 0);
    setTimeout(function(){ cm.refresh(); }, 350);

    hintBtn.onclick = function() {
      hint.classList.toggle('show');
    };

    if (cm.getOption('lineWrapping')) { wrapBtn.className = 'csa-ce-wrapbtn on'; wrapBtn.innerHTML = 'Wrap: on'; }
    wrapBtn.onclick = function() {
      var on = !cm.getOption('lineWrapping');
      cm.setOption('lineWrapping', on);
      wrapBtn.className = on ? 'csa-ce-wrapbtn on' : 'csa-ce-wrapbtn';
      wrapBtn.innerHTML = on ? 'Wrap: on' : 'Wrap lines';
      cm.refresh();
    };

    resetBtn.onclick = function() {
      cm.setValue(p.starter);
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';
    };

    runBtn.onclick = function() {
      var code = cm.getValue();

        return;
      }
      CSACE_RUNS++;
      runBtn.disabled = true;
      status.textContent = 'Compiling and running...';
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';

      nativeFetch(PROXY_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ code: code, lessonId: lessonId, problemId: p.id })
      })
      .then(function(res) {
        return res.json().then(function(data) {
          return { ok: res.ok, status: res.status, data: data };
        });
      })
      .then(function(result) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        var data = result.data;

        if (!result.ok) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = data.message || 'Run failed. Try again.';
          return;
        }

        if (data.compile_output) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Compile error:\n' + data.compile_output;
          return;
        }

        if (data.stderr) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Runtime error:\n' + data.stderr;
          return;
        }

        var stdout = data.stdout || '';

        if (p.expected === null || p.expected === undefined) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show plain';
          out.textContent = 'Output:\n' + (stdout || '(no output)');
          return;
        }

        if (normalize(stdout) === normalize(p.expected)) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show ok';
          if (window.APCS_reportAttempt) { APCS_reportAttempt({ item_id: lessonId + '-code-1', item_type: 'cfu', score: 1, max_score: 1, detail: [{ q: idx + 1, sel: null, ok: true }] }); }
          out.textContent = '✓ Correct!\nOutput: ' + stdout.replace(/\n$/, '');
        } else {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = '✗ Not quite.\nYour output: ' + (stdout.replace(/\n$/, '') || '(none)') + '\nExpected: ' + p.expected;
        }
      })
      .catch(function(err) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
        out.textContent = 'Could not reach the code runner. Check your connection and try again.';
      });
    };
  }

  function init() {
    for (var i = 0; i < CSACE_PROBLEMS.length; i++) {

  if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);

<section class="apcsa-practice-tier">
  <h2>
<span class="tier-label">Tier 2 Practice</span> Check your understanding</h2>
  <p style="font-size: 15px !important; color: #475569 !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #475569 !important;">

  <!-- EX 1: I/II/III multi-correct, answer C -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="C" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-1">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Multi-select stem</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>1.</strong> A student is writing an algorithm to make oatmeal. Consider the following statements about algorithms and sequencing.
      <ol style="margin-top: 10px !important; padding-left: 24px !important;">
        <li>An algorithm can be represented in written language, in a diagram, or in code, and the representation does not change whether the algorithm is correct.</li>
        <li>Reordering two steps in an algorithm always produces a different result.</li>
        <li>An algorithm only counts as “an algorithm” once it is written in a programming language; a recipe on paper does not qualify.</li>
      </ol>
      Which of the statements are true?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> I only</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> I and II</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> I only is fully correct; II and III are false</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> II and III</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>C.</strong> Only statement I is true: the CED explicitly says algorithms can be represented in written language, diagrams, or code, and correctness is independent of representation. Statement II overreaches, reordering two steps <em>can</em> change the result, but if the two steps are independent (e.g., “put on left sock” then “put on right sock”) the result is identical. Statement III is the most common student mistake: a paper recipe and a flowchart are perfectly valid algorithm representations, nothing about the definition requires code.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 2: NOT/EXCEPT spot the misconception, predict-gate ON, answer D -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="D" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-2">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Spot the misconception</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>2.</strong> Which of the following statements about compilers and errors is <strong>NOT</strong> true?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">This stem uses <strong>NOT</strong>. You’re looking for the option that is <em>wrong</em>. Before reading the choices, predict what a compiler can and cannot catch. Then read all four.</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> A program that fails to compile will not run at all until the errors are fixed.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> Syntax errors are violations of the rules of the programming language and are detected by the compiler.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A program can compile successfully and still produce incorrect output for some inputs.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> If a program compiles successfully, then it will never throw a run-time exception during execution.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>D.</strong> Option D is the false statement, successful compilation means only that the code follows Java’s language rules, not that it is safe at run time. A compiled program can still throw exceptions like <code>ArithmeticException</code> (division by zero) or <code>NullPointerException</code> the moment it tries an operation the compiler couldn’t predict. A, B, and C are all accurate: compile failures block execution, syntax errors are language-rule violations the compiler catches, and clean compilation says nothing about logical correctness.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 3: Matching -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="matching" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-3">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Matching</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>3.</strong> Match each error type on the left to its precise definition on the right.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-matching">
      <div class="apcs-match-col">
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t1"><strong>Syntax error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t2"><strong>Logic error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t3"><strong>Run-time error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t4"><strong>Exception</strong></div>
      </div>
      <div class="apcs-match-col">
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t3">An error that occurs during program execution, typically causing the program to terminate abnormally.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t1">A violation of the rules of the programming language; detected by the compiler before the program runs.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t4">A type of run-time error from an unexpected condition the compiler did not detect, interrupting normal flow.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t2">A mistake in the algorithm itself; the program runs but produces incorrect or unexpected results.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check matches</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      Syntax errors live entirely at compile time. Logic errors run cleanly but give wrong answers (think: off-by-one bug in a loop). Run-time errors halt execution mid-program. Exceptions are the specific subset of run-time errors that occur because of unexpected conditions like dividing by zero, every exception is a run-time error, but not every run-time error is an exception.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 4: Scenario sort (3 buckets: syntax / logic / run-time) -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="scenario-sort" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-4">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Classify</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>4.</strong> For each scenario below, classify the error as a syntax error, a logic error, or a run-time error.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-sort-bank">
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b1">A student forgets the semicolon at the end of <code>int x = 5</code> and the program will not compile.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b2">A program that computes the average of three test scores returns the sum instead because the student forgot to divide by 3.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b3">A program crashes with <code>ArithmeticException</code> when the user enters 0 as the divisor.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b1">A student types <code>Sytem.out.println</code> with a misspelled class name and the IDE underlines it in red before running.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b2">A loop intended to print numbers 1 through 10 prints 0 through 9 because the student started the counter at the wrong value.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b3">A program that reads a file crashes partway through with <code>NullPointerException</code> the first time it encounters an empty line.</div>
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-sort-buckets">
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b1"><h5>Syntax error</h5></div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b2"><h5>Logic error</h5></div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b3"><h5>Run-time error</h5></div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check sorting</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      The two syntax errors (missing semicolon, misspelled <code>System</code>) are caught by the compiler, so the program never runs. The two logic errors compile and run but produce wrong output: in both cases Java did exactly what was written, which wasn’t what the student meant. The two run-time errors (division by zero, null pointer) compile cleanly and execute until they hit a condition the compiler couldn’t predict.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 5: Cloze -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="cloze" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-5">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Cloze · Vocabulary in context</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>5.</strong> Fill each blank with the correct term from the bank below.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-cloze-text">
      A student writes a Java program in their
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="IDE"></span>,
      saves the file, and clicks Run. The
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="compiler"></span>
      reports no errors, so the program starts executing. After thirty seconds it terminates abnormally with a stack trace; this is a
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="run-time error"></span>.
      The student fixes the crash, runs the program again, and this time it finishes cleanly but produces the wrong answer for several inputs. This second problem is a
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="logic error"></span>.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-cloze-chips">
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="IDE">IDE</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="compiler">compiler</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="run-time error">run-time error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="logic error">logic error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="syntax error">syntax error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="algorithm">algorithm</span>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answers</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      The IDE is where code is written and managed. The compiler is the gatekeeper before execution; if it reports no errors, syntax is not the problem. A program that compiles but terminates abnormally during execution is hitting a run-time error. A program that compiles, runs to completion, and produces wrong output has a logic error. The algorithm itself is flawed.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 6: Applied scenario, answer A -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="A" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-6">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Applied scenario</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>6.</strong> A student writes a Java program that calculates a tip on a restaurant bill. The program compiles without any errors and runs to completion every time, but the tip amount is consistently 10 times larger than it should be. Which of the following best classifies this mistake?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> A logic error, because the program runs without crashing but produces an incorrect result.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> A syntax error, because the program is using the wrong math operator and the compiler should have caught it.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A run-time error, because the wrong value appears during execution rather than at compile time.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> An exception, because the output deviates from what was expected.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>A.</strong> The defining feature here is that the program compiles, runs to completion, and produces incorrect output, and that is the textbook signature of a logic error. B is wrong because the compiler does not check whether math is “correct” for your purposes; multiplying by 10 instead of 0.1 is valid Java. C is the most attractive trap: a run-time error specifically means execution is interrupted (the program terminates abnormally), which is not what happened. D is wrong because an exception is a specific kind of run-time error, not a generic label for any incorrect output.
    </div>
  </div>

<h2>Common AP exam traps</h2>
<p>The exam predictably tests these same misconceptions year after year. Recognize them now and you’ll catch them in May.</p>
<div class="apcsa-traps">
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 1: “If it compiles, it works”</h4>
    <p>Successful compilation means the code follows Java’s rules, nothing more. A compiled program can still throw exceptions at run time or produce completely wrong output. The compiler is one layer of error detection, not the only layer.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 2: Confusing exception with run-time error</h4>
    <p>Students often treat “exception” and “run-time error” as synonyms. An exception is a <em>specific kind</em> of run-time error caused by an unexpected condition the compiler did not detect. All exceptions are run-time errors, but not all run-time errors are exceptions.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 3: Logic errors classified as something else</h4>
    <p>If a program compiles, runs to completion, and produces wrong output, it is still a logic error, even when the wrong output seems “weird” or “unexpected.” The exam will phrase the scenario in ways that tempt you to call it an exception. Don’t.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 4: “An algorithm has to be in code”</h4>
    <p>The CED explicitly lists written language and diagrams as valid algorithm representations. A flowchart, a numbered list of steps, and a Java method are all algorithms; the form of representation has nothing to do with whether the algorithm is correct.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<section class="apcsa-extension">
  <span class="ext-badge">Tier 4 · Beyond AP (Optional)</span>
  <h3>How real compilers find more than just syntax errors</h3>
  <p>Modern compilers and IDEs go well beyond the bare minimum the AP exam describes. Java’s compiler also performs <em>type checking</em> (catching mismatches like assigning a <code>String</code> to an <code>int</code>) and <em>definite assignment analysis</em> (refusing to compile if a local variable might be used before it’s assigned). IntelliJ and Eclipse add static analysis on top of that, flagging suspicious patterns, unused variables, methods that always return the same value, possible null dereferences, before you even hit Run. Some of these warnings catch genuine logic errors before they ever execute. None of this is on the AP exam, but it’s worth knowing that the line between “compile-time” and “run-time” is blurrier in professional tools than the CED’s clean four-category framework suggests.</p>
  <p style="font-size: 14px !important; color: #6b21a8 !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #6b21a8 !important; font-style: italic !important;">
    This material extends beyond the AP CSA curriculum. Skip it if you’re focused on exam prep.
  </p>
</section>

(function() {
  document.querySelectorAll('#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex').forEach(function(ex) {

    ex.dataset.mcqInit = '1';
    var correct = ex.getAttribute('data-answer');
    var opts = ex.querySelectorAll('.apcs-opt');
    var btn = ex.querySelector('.apcs-ex-check');
    var feedback = ex.querySelector('.apcs-ex-feedback');
    var chosen = null;

    opts.forEach(function(opt) {
      opt.style.cursor = 'pointer';
      opt.addEventListener('click', function() {
        if (ex.dataset.answered) return;
        opts.forEach(function(o) { o.classList.remove('selected'); });
        opt.classList.add('selected');
        chosen = opt.getAttribute('data-letter');
      });
    });

    if (btn) btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
      if (!chosen || ex.dataset.answered) return;
      ex.dataset.answered = '1';
      opts.forEach(function(opt) {
        var letter = opt.getAttribute('data-letter');
        if (letter === correct) opt.classList.add('correct');
        else if (letter === chosen) opt.classList.add('incorrect');
        opt.classList.remove('selected');
      });
      if (feedback) {
        feedback.classList.add('show');
        feedback.classList.add(chosen === correct ? 'fb-correct' : 'fb-incorrect');
      }
      btn.disabled = true;
    });
  });
})();
</script>

5.1 Checkpoint: Application & Data Vulnerabilities

Five questions. Harder than the lesson examples. Each one tests a distinction the AP exam loves to exploit: Broken Auth vs Access Control, Injection vs Sensitive Data Exposure, right-layer vs wrong-layer controls.

5 Questions ~10 min Scored Exam-style

How to Approach

Predict-first: read each question, commit to a category, then look at options. The AP exam includes plausible-sounding wrong answers precisely to catch students who let options shape their thinking.

Watch for trap distractors: wrong-layer controls (firewalls for application attacks), wrong-category labels (Broken Auth vs Broken Access Control), and symptom fixes (changing passwords when sessions were stolen).

5.3 Checkpoint: Hashing for Data Integrity

Five exam-style questions. Each tests a distinction the AP exam loves: hash vs encrypt, fast hash vs slow hash, plain hash vs HMAC, high-entropy vs low-entropy data, collision resistance vs pre-image resistance.

5 Questions~10 minScored · Exam-style

How to Approach

Predict-first: For each scenario, categorize the use case (file integrity / password storage / API authentication / signature / low-entropy data).

Remember: SHA-256 is fast (good for files, bad for passwords). bcrypt/Argon2 is slow (good for passwords). HMAC adds authenticity. Encryption reverses; hashing does not. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

5.4 Checkpoint: Asymmetric Cryptography & PKI

Five exam-style questions on the highest-tested distinctions in this lesson: which key does what, PKI chain of trust, certificate pinning, lifecycle management, and the post-quantum transition.

5 Questions~10 minScored · Exam-style

How to Approach

Predict first: For each scenario, decide what the question is really testing (which key / which validation step / which operational control).

Remember the four truths: (1) public keys are public, (2) hybrid crypto is standard, (3) PKI trust fails at any broken link, (4) post-quantum migration is hybrid and ongoing.

L5.5 Exam-Style Quiz

Five exam-format questions across all L5.5 topics: defense in depth, secure coding, input validation, output encoding, authentication and session controls, CSP, WAF, and rate limiting. Mix of spot-the-error, I/II/III multi-correct, and scenario-based stems — exactly the formats you will see on the AP exam.

5 Questions ~12 min Exam Format

How to Approach These

1. Identify the OWASP category from the stem before reading options.

2. For I/II/III questions, evaluate each statement independently. Do not anchor on the first true statement.

3. For code questions, trace what happens line by line. Look for trusted-input-into-interpreter patterns, denylist filters, and fail-open logic.

4. Prefer root-cause controls over compensating controls. Parameterized queries, MFA, encoding, and session regeneration beat WAFs, CAPTCHAs, and signature-based filters.
